items.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001
items.q: And Billy asked me to open Birdland with him and make all these gigs, and be a steady member of his trio

ctx.x: From a business and economic standpoint, was it a decent living for you in those years, in the 50s?

Oh yeah. I’ll tell you why, because not being trained at all, not playing the bass left handed like that, I couldn’t study formally or anything like that. So I just wound up saying to myself I’m going to have a day job during the week, I don’t know, five days a week or whatever, and I’ll work on the weekends just playing weddings and bar mitzvahs and things like that. And then actually Billy Taylor was the one that made the decision for me, because I’m thinking that I’m just married and I’ve got a young baby you…

don’t know, I don’t know. I don’t want to have to scuffle. And finally I just took a chance. My wife game me an opportunity. She said well you just follow your mind. I’m very happy I did that because on the weekends I would make three times the money I would make on my day job, working for an insurance company at that time and playing, like I said, playing with all these other people. So financially it was really very good. But my wife at that time told me that I was too giving. I’m always giving my money away…

items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: the trio was Earl May and Charlie Smith. And we worked together for a long time.

ctx.x: Yeah give me the current… because we left it…

My first, really when I began to support a trio and began to get out there with a trio, the trio was Earl May and Charlie Smith. And we worked together for a long time. But Charlie Smith unfortunately had a drinking habit and so he had the dubious distinction of having been hired and fired by every major pianist in jazz, literally. I mean there was hardly a pianist that you couldn’t mention, Earl Garner, Oscar Peterson, Art Tatum, Duke Ellington I mean there was no one you could mention that he hadn’t played with…

and I don’t… it doesn’t sound right with me.” He said, “I can do that.” I said, “Well you don’t have a Congo drum.” He said, “Yeah but I can do that.” So he took the mallet and began [music sounds] and he invented that in that context. Nobody had done that before Charlie Smith. And the reason he did it because he wanted me to play this tune. And ultimately he got a Congo drum and put that in between… he would move his snare over and play the Congo and work both feet and use his hands on the Congo and do like…
